title: Investigate work opportunities in order to make a personal employment or work decision

lessons.title: Knowing yourself and finding work opportunities
lessons.html:
Start with yourself

Before you look for a new job or decide on a career step, look at yourself honestly. A good work decision fits your skills, interests, values and life situation.

  • Skills: What can you do well? For example: grooming, lungeing, riding work, driving a tractor, reading a feed chart, leading a team.
  • Interests: What do you enjoy? Working with racehorses, breeding stock, show horses, or maybe tourism such as trail riding?
  • Qualifications: What certificates do you have? Which unit standards have you completed?
  • Values and needs: Do you need to live near your family? Do you want accommodation on the farm? Do you need a fixed salary, or are you willing to earn commission or tips?

The equine industry in South Africa

There are many kinds of work with horses:

SectorExample jobs
RacingGroom, work rider, apprentice jockey, travelling head groom, assistant trainer
Stud farmsStud groom, foaling attendant, yard supervisor
Sport and showingGroom for show jumping, dressage or endurance yards
Riding schools and tourismStable hand, trail guide, riding instructor assistant
ServicesFarrier assistant, saddlery, feed sales, veterinary practice assistant
WelfareAnimal welfare organisations working with working horses and donkeys

Where to find opportunities

  • Word of mouth: tell people in the industry you are looking
  • Notices at feed stores, racecourses, the co-op and vet practices
  • Newspapers and online job sites
  • Training providers and learnerships through the AgriSETA
  • The Department of Employment and Labour's labour centres

Be careful of job scams. A real employer does not ask you to pay money to get a job.

lessons.title: Comparing options and making a decision
lessons.html:
Gather information

For each opportunity, find out the facts. Ask questions politely, or speak to people who work there.

  • What are the duties and working hours, including weekends and race days?
  • What is the pay? Is it weekly or monthly? Are there overtime and bonuses?
  • Is accommodation, transport or food provided?
  • Is there training and a chance to grow?
  • Is the job permanent, seasonal or a contract?
  • How far is it from your family?

Compare your options

Make a simple table. Give each point a score from 1 (poor) to 5 (good).

FactorJob A: Stud groomJob B: Racing groom
Pay34
Hours42
Accommodation53
Training and growth35
Near family42
Total1916

The totals help, but think about which factors matter most to you. If growth is very important, Job B may still be better.

Making the decision

  1. List your options.
  2. Write the advantages and disadvantages of each.
  3. Talk to people you trust: family, a mentor, your supervisor.
  4. Decide, and write down why.
  5. Make a plan: when you will apply, what you need (CV, ID copy, certificates, references).

Preparing to apply

  • A short CV: name, contact details, skills, work history, training, two references.
  • Certified copies of your ID and certificates.
  • For an interview: arrive on time, dress neatly, take your documents, answer honestly.

Leaving a job properly

If you accept a new job, give your current employer the notice in your contract, in writing. Leave on good terms; you may need a reference later.

Key points

  • Know your skills, interests, qualifications and needs.
  • The equine industry offers work in racing, studs, sport, tourism, services and welfare.
  • Gather facts on pay, hours, accommodation and growth.
  • Compare options in a table and talk to people you trust.
  • Never pay money to get a job; give proper notice when you leave.
